title: Why cities keep growing
paras: The standard account of urban growth treats the city as a bargain struck with open eyes. Workers accept dearer housing, longer commutes and dirtier air because wages in dense places run well above those elsewhere; firms accept the same bargain because proximity lowers the cost of finding workers, suppliers and customers. Economists call the benefit agglomeration and, having named it, tend to stop. The label describes a correlation rather than a mechanism, and it conceals a question that matters for policy: whether the premium that cities pay is a reward for being there or a reward for being a certain kind of person who happens to be there.

The distinction is not pedantic. Cities attract the ambitious and the able, so a simple comparison of urban and rural earnings will overstate what the city itself contributes; an exceptional engineer would earn a great deal wherever she lived. Researchers have therefore followed individuals over time rather than comparing places, and their findings are curious. Newcomers from small towns earn little extra in their first years, yet their wages then rise more steeply than those of similar workers who stayed behind, and some of the gain persists, in diminished form, among those who later leave. A subsidy tied to location would vanish with departure; what survives departure looks more like accumulated skill. On this reading, the city works less as a market than as a school whose fees are collected in rent.

Yet the schooling metaphor invites scepticism of its own. Skills acquired through casual contact are notoriously hard to observe, and the studies that infer them do so by elimination: whatever remains of the premium after other explanations have been subtracted is credited to learning. If that residue is partly the product of unmeasured traits, such as persistence or useful acquaintances, the conclusion weakens accordingly. Nor does the evidence say how large the benefits become as cities swell. The little that is known suggests that they rise with population at a falling rate, whereas the price of land, which is what rent ultimately reflects, rises with scarcity and need not slow at all. A city may therefore be too small to exploit its advantages and, beyond some point, too large to enjoy them; where that point lies the data do not reveal.

What follows for policy is less obvious than either side of the debate supposes. Those who would cap the size of great cities treat congestion as a bill to be reduced; those who would lift every restriction on building treat the premium as proof that more room is always better. Neither position follows from the evidence. If the gains come from learning, however, they accrue chiefly to the young and the mobile, who are precisely the people that rising rents exclude first. Restricting construction in productive places would then act as a tax on acquiring skill, one whose burden falls on those with least to spare and whose proceeds are collected by owners of existing property. Because no ledger records skills never acquired, the tax is easy to deny and hard to abolish.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best expresses the central concern of the passage?

options.t: The urban wage premium is largely a statistical illusion created by the migration of talented people, so housing policy has little bearing on productivity.
options.why: The author grants that selection inflates simple comparisons, but cites evidence that something beyond selection remains (paragraph 2), and then draws a policy implication from it.

options.t: The urban wage premium may partly reflect skills gained in cities, making building restrictions a hidden cost, though ideal city size remains unknown.
options.why: This joins the learning interpretation of the premium (paragraphs 1 and 2) with the policy cost of restricting building (paragraph 4), and keeps the author's hedge that the right size of a city is not revealed by the data (paragraph 3).

options.t: Agglomeration is a well-established mechanism, so great cities should be allowed to expand until the cost of congestion exactly matches the benefit of density.
options.why: Paragraph 1 calls the label a description of a correlation, not a mechanism, and paragraph 4 says neither side's policy position follows from the evidence.

options.t: Learning in cities is inferred by elimination, so the urban wage premium says more about who moves to cities than about what cities do for them.
options.why: The first half is the author's caution (paragraph 3), but the author still treats the learning reading as plausible and builds the policy argument of paragraph 4 on it; this turns a caution into a verdict.

questions.stem: The author describes the city as 'a school whose fees are collected in rent' in order to:

options.t: suggest that urban rents are best understood as payment for an education that universities have failed to provide.
options.why: No comparison with universities is made; the metaphor concerns skills picked up through contact with other workers.

options.t: suggest that newcomers gain mainly through experience at work, which smaller towns would supply as well if their firms were larger.
options.why: The passage compares movers with similar workers who stayed behind, so it credits the city, not experience at work in general; firm size in small towns is never discussed.

options.t: suggest that high rents push workers to learn faster, since they must earn more in order to afford to stay.
options.why: In the metaphor rent is the price paid for the learning, not its cause; the passage never says that rents make workers learn.

options.t: express a reading on which what workers gain in cities is portable skill, with housing costs as the price.
options.why: If part of the premium survives departure, the gain is skill rather than subsidy, and rent is what the worker pays to acquire it (paragraph 2).

questions.stem: The passage mentions all of the following as reasons for caution about the claim that cities raise wages by teaching workers EXCEPT:

options.t: better communications have narrowed the earnings gap between city and countryside over recent decades.
options.why: Nothing in the passage discusses communications technology or any narrowing of the gap between city and countryside.

options.t: the premium that remains once other explanations are removed is attributed to learning by default.
options.why: Paragraph 3: learning is inferred by elimination, which is a source of doubt.

options.t: talented and ambitious people are drawn to cities, which inflates simple comparisons of earnings.
options.why: Paragraph 2: selection means a simple comparison overstates what the city itself contributes.

options.t: unmeasured traits such as persistence and contacts may account for part of what is credited to learning.
options.why: Paragraph 3: the residue may be partly the product of unmeasured traits.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's suggestion that restrictions on building act as a tax on acquiring skill?

options.t: Workers who leave the largest cities after several years keep only a diminished part of the premium they earned while living there.
options.why: The author already reports this finding (paragraph 2), and it fits the learning claim rather than weakening it.

options.t: Owners of property in cities with strict building rules report higher incomes than owners of property in cities that build freely.
options.why: This bears on who collects the proceeds, not on whether exclusion costs workers skill; if anything it is consistent with the author's picture.

options.t: Young workers priced out of the largest cities mostly move to slightly smaller ones, where wages rise at nearly the same pace.
options.why: If excluded workers learn almost as fast elsewhere, rising rents do little to reduce skill acquisition, and the supposed tax shrinks.

options.t: Congestion costs in the largest cities have, as populations have grown, risen faster than the benefits that density brings to firms.
options.why: This concerns the balance of costs and benefits (paragraph 3), which the author already treats as uncertain; it says nothing about who is excluded.

recall.q: Why have researchers followed individual workers over time instead of comparing places?
options: Regional wage statistics for small towns are unreliable because very few firms report what they pay.
Comparing places cannot separate what a city adds from the qualities of the people it attracts.
Workers in small towns are reluctant to disclose their earnings to the researchers conducting surveys.
A comparison of places would have required data on local rents, which researchers could not obtain.

recall.q: According to the passage, how do the wages of newcomers from small towns behave?
options: They jump on arrival and then level off to match those of established city workers.
They rise only for workers who stay in the city throughout their careers.
They fall at first because of high rents and later recover to their earlier level.
They begin near comparable workers' wages, then climb faster, and the gain partly survives departure.

title: The paradox of thrift
paras: Moralists have always found thrift easy to praise, and economists have found it hardly harder, so long as the thrifty are considered one at a time. A household that spends less than it earns acquires a cushion against misfortune; a country whose households all do so appears to acquire a fund from which factories can be built. It was against this comfortable symmetry that Keynes directed what later came to be called the paradox of thrift. Suppose that, alarmed by the prospect of unemployment, everyone tries to save more at once. One household's thrift is another household's lost custom. Shops sell less, payrolls shrink, and the incomes out of which the extra saving was to come contract with them. The attempt to add to the nation's savings may leave them no larger than before; what was prudent in each case proves futile in the aggregate.

The paradox is easily mistaken for a claim that saving is harmful, which it is not. Its target is narrower: the assumption that an economy's willingness to save will automatically be matched by its willingness to invest. In the classical picture the assumption is secured by the interest rate. If households save more, the price of borrowing falls until firms are tempted to borrow the surplus, and what was withheld from consumption returns as investment. Nothing in this picture is incoherent; it is a statement about how quickly prices adjust. Keynes's point was that in a slump they may not adjust quickly enough, or far enough, since a firm with idle machinery has little reason to borrow at any rate, and the rate itself cannot fall below zero.

Defenders of the older view were not silenced by this reply. They observed that the paradox, taken seriously, proves too much: if the shortfall in demand were self-perpetuating, no economy could recover without outside help, yet recoveries have usually come. The likelier explanation, they argued, is that wages and prices do eventually adjust, so that the paradox describes a transition and not a trap. This is a fair objection, and it explains why much of the dispute has concerned duration rather than direction. Keynesians do not deny that adjustment occurs; they deny that it is quick or painless enough to be left alone, and they note that the years after 2008, when households, firms and governments in many countries tried to reduce their debts together, were years in which growth was slow to return.

The policy conclusion commonly drawn from all this, that governments should spend while others save and retrench once private demand revives, deserves the same measured treatment. It rests on a symmetry that rarely survives contact with politics. An expansion is simple to begin, since it distributes benefits to identifiable groups, whereas a contraction takes those benefits away and must be enforced against organised resistance. The paradox can therefore explain why austerity in a slump may defeat its own purpose, without guaranteeing that the remedy it recommends will be withdrawn when its work is done. What appears in the textbook as a temporary counter-cyclical device may in practice become a standing commitment, and an argument for stimulus in bad years becomes, unannounced, an argument for deficits in every year.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best summarises the author's position?

options.t: The paradox of thrift shows that saving by households is harmful and should be discouraged by public policy whenever incomes across the economy are falling.
options.why: Paragraph 2 says the paradox is easily mistaken for exactly such a claim, and that it is not one.

options.t: Because prices eventually adjust, the paradox describes a transition rather than a trap, and the author's main worry is that austerity in a slump prolongs it.
options.why: The first half restates the critics' objection, which the author grants, but the summary leaves out the author's doubt that stimulus, once begun, will be withdrawn (paragraph 4), the point the passage ends on.

options.t: The paradox identifies a conditional failure to match saving with investment; it supports counter-cyclical spending in principle but not that stimulus will end.
options.why: This combines the narrow target of the paradox (paragraph 2), its conditional character (paragraph 3) and the doubt about whether stimulus is ever withdrawn (paragraph 4).

options.t: Saving by households and firms deepens a slump only when governments are cutting their debts too, as happened in many countries after 2008.
options.why: Paragraph 3 cites the years after 2008 as an example of everyone cutting debts together, not as a condition without which saving is harmless; the paradox works through private saving alone.

questions.stem: The author regards the objection that the paradox 'proves too much' as:

options.t: a fair point that moves the dispute from whether the paradox operates to its duration.
options.why: Paragraph 3 calls it a fair objection and says the dispute has concerned duration rather than direction.

options.t: a serious objection that the Keynesian reply leaves unanswered, since that reply concedes that recoveries usually come.
options.why: The author says the reply answers it by moving the dispute to duration: conceding that recovery comes is compatible with denying that it comes quickly or painlessly.

options.t: a misreading of Keynes, whose argument concerned how far interest rates can fall rather than whether recoveries occur.
options.why: The author calls the objection fair, not a misreading, and the floor on interest rates is only one of Keynes's reasons why saving may not become investment.

options.t: an objection that damages the classical view of interest rates at least as much as the Keynesian view.
options.why: Nothing in the passage suggests the objection counts against the classical view.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is a reason why saving may fail to turn into investment in a slump EXCEPT:

options.t: wages and prices may adjust too slowly or too little to restore demand.
options.why: Paragraph 2: in a slump prices may not adjust quickly enough, or far enough.

options.t: there is a floor below which the rate of interest cannot be pushed.
options.why: Paragraph 2: the rate itself cannot fall below zero.

options.t: firms with idle machinery see little point in borrowing at any rate.
options.why: Paragraph 2 says a firm with idle machinery has little reason to borrow at any rate.

options.t: banks tighten their lending standards when households increase their savings.
options.why: Bank behaviour is never discussed; the passage locates the blockage in firms' demand for funds and in prices that adjust slowly.

questions.stem: The author's attitude towards the policy conclusion drawn from the paradox is best described as:

options.t: approval of its logic, qualified only by a worry about the administrative burden of spending.
options.why: The reservation is political, about reversing spending once begun, not about administration.

options.t: acceptance of its logic in principle, with doubt about its working in practice.
options.why: The author says the paradox explains why austerity can defeat itself, but doubts that the remedy will be withdrawn when its work is done (paragraph 4).

options.t: scepticism about its premise, since the author sides with the critics who hold that slumps correct themselves.
options.why: The author grants that adjustment occurs but accepts that slumps can persist; the doubt is about withdrawing stimulus later, not about the premise.

options.t: detachment from its political consequences, which are placed beyond the scope of economics itself.
options.why: The political consequences are the whole subject of the final paragraph.

recall.q: What does the paradox, as the author presents it, actually challenge?
options: The belief that households should keep a cushion against misfortune in hard times.
The practice of governments borrowing heavily during a recession to support demand.
The assumption that saving will automatically be matched by investment.
The claim that interest rates influence firms' decisions about whether to borrow.

recall.q: What, according to the author, makes the textbook symmetry of stimulus and retrenchment hard to sustain?
options: Spending gives benefits to identifiable groups, so withdrawing it meets organised resistance.
Spending is administratively costlier to stop than retrenchment is to start.
Retrenchment always lowers interest rates and so revives private demand.
Governments are legally unable to reduce spending once a slump has ended.

title: Rules or discretion
paras: The oldest argument for letting central bankers use their judgment is also the most persuasive: no formula composed in advance can anticipate the shocks an economy will deliver, and a rule that is sensible in ordinary times may prove perverse in extraordinary ones. Judgment adapts where rules cannot. Against this, economists who made their names in the 1970s raised an objection that has nothing to do with the intelligence of central bankers. A bank that can alter its course at will is, for that very reason, difficult to believe. If it announces that it will hold inflation down, wage-setters have reason to suspect that it will weaken once they and their employers have committed themselves to contracts, because a burst of surprise inflation yields a temporary gain in employment that a tempted official may find hard to resist.

The suspicion, once formed, is self-fulfilling. Wage-setters who expect the bank to yield will build higher inflation into their demands in advance, so that the bank, confronted with costs already raised, can avoid a recession only by validating them. Inflation settles at a higher level and employment gains nothing, since the surprise on which the gain depended has been anticipated. The analysis is striking because it requires neither folly nor bad faith on the part of the bank; it requires only that the bank be free to reconsider and that the public know it. The remedy therefore lies not in better decisions but in better commitments.

Two commitments were tried. The first, a binding rule that fixes the response of interest rates to inflation and output, removes the temptation by removing the choice, at the price of the flexibility that made discretion attractive in the first place. The second, which governments in most rich countries eventually adopted, delegates the decision to an official body shielded from electoral pressure, with a numerical target and an obligation to explain departures from it. This arrangement keeps judgment but disciplines it, and it works only to the extent that the public believes the discipline to be real. That belief is an asset of a peculiar kind, laboriously accumulated and quickly squandered: a central bank that has spent a generation establishing its resolve may forfeit it in a single misjudged episode, whereas a newer institution may have to pay for credibility it has not yet earned.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that credibility settles the matter. Independence resolves one problem by creating another: the power to set interest rates, which affect the livelihoods of millions, is handed to officials whom no electorate can dismiss, and their legitimacy rests on a presumption that technical and political questions can be cleanly separated. In periods of acute strain that presumption becomes difficult to sustain. When central banks buy government debt on a vast scale, or hold rates near zero for years, their choices have distributional effects that look very like fiscal policy, and critics ask, with some justice, why the unelected should be making them. A bank that is believed may nonetheless find that it is no longer trusted to decide.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best captures the author's central argument?

options.t: Central banks should be bound by fixed rules, since the case for discretion collapses once the public anticipates how officials will behave.
options.why: Paragraph 3 says a binding rule gives up the flexibility that made discretion attractive; the author does not recommend it.

options.t: Inflation in the 1970s resulted from officials willing to sacrifice price stability for employment, a failing that independence has since removed.
options.why: Paragraph 2 says the analysis needs neither folly nor bad faith, and paragraph 4 shows that independence brings problems of its own.

options.t: The credibility of a central bank depends chiefly on the length of its record, so newer institutions are bound to perform worse than established ones.
options.why: Record length is mentioned in paragraph 3 as one part of how credibility is built; it is neither the chief factor nor a guarantee of worse performance.

options.t: Independent central banks answer the problem of credibility but bring a problem of legitimacy that credibility itself cannot resolve.
options.why: Paragraphs 2 and 3 set out the credibility problem and its institutional answer; paragraph 4 argues that the answer creates a legitimacy problem of its own.

questions.stem: According to the second paragraph, the outcome of 'higher inflation with no gain in employment' arises because:

options.t: officials misjudge how interest rates affect employment and so choose a course that damages both inflation and jobs.
options.why: Paragraph 2 says the analysis requires neither folly nor bad faith on the part of the bank.

options.t: the public correctly anticipates the bank's incentive to yield, removing the surprise on which an employment gain depends.
options.why: Because the temptation is anticipated and built into wage demands, inflation rises, but the employment gain, which needed a surprise, never arrives.

options.t: wage-setters are slow to learn what the bank intends and keep basing their demands on past inflation.
options.why: Wage-setters in paragraph 2 correctly anticipate the bank's incentive; the trouble is that they understand it too well, not too slowly.

options.t: the bank, having announced a target, is prevented by law from adjusting rates once wages begin to rise.
options.why: The problem arises from the bank's freedom to reconsider, not from any legal restriction.

questions.stem: The passage mentions all of the following as features of the arrangements it describes EXCEPT:

options.t: a binding rule gives up the flexibility that made discretion attractive.
options.why: Paragraph 3: a rule removes the temptation by removing the choice, at that price.

options.t: an independent bank must explain its departures from a numerical target.
options.why: Paragraph 3: independence comes with a numerical target and an obligation to explain departures.

options.t: rule-following banks are judged more harshly by markets than discretionary ones.
options.why: The passage never compares how markets judge rule-following and discretionary banks.

options.t: a newer institution may have to pay for credibility it has not yet earned.
options.why: Paragraph 3 states this in its final sentence.

questions.stem: Which of the following developments would most strengthen the author's concern about the legitimacy of independent central banks?

options.t: Elected legislators widely denounce a central bank's years of near-zero interest rates as favouring asset owners over wage earners.
options.why: This shows technical decisions acquiring distributional effects that elected officials contest, which is exactly the pattern paragraph 4 describes.

options.t: A central bank with a long record of meeting its target narrowly misses it in one year and publishes a detailed explanation.
options.why: A transparent response to a small miss is the discipline paragraph 3 describes; it does not raise the legitimacy problem.

options.t: A newly established central bank adopts a numerical target and finds that wage-setters are slow to believe it.
options.why: This illustrates the credibility problem of paragraph 3, not the legitimacy problem of paragraph 4.

options.t: A government replaces the head of its central bank at the end of a fixed, non-renewable term.
options.why: An orderly change of leadership says nothing about whether the unelected should make distributional choices.

recall.q: According to the passage, what do wage-setters do if they expect the bank to yield?
options: Delay wage agreements until the bank announces its target.
Accept lower wages in return for guaranteed employment.
Rely on the bank's announcement and keep their demands unchanged.
Build higher inflation into their demands in advance.

recall.q: What is the price of a binding rule, as the author describes it?
options: It lowers inflation at the cost of higher unemployment.
It gives up the flexibility that made discretion attractive.
It places the central bank under the control of elected governments.
It makes the bank's target impossible to explain in public.

title: When buyers cannot see quality
paras: The market for used cars has become the standard illustration of what happens when one party to a transaction knows more than the other. The seller knows the history of the vehicle; the buyer can inspect only its paintwork. Wary, the buyer will pay no more than the price of an average car, and this offer insults the owners of better-than-average ones, who withdraw. The average quality of the cars still for sale then declines, the offer falls, and the process repeats. In the limit only the worst cars remain, and an exchange that would have profited sellers and buyers alike never takes place. When George Akerlof set out this argument in 1970, journals that thought it trivial turned it down. The verdict has not worn well.

Yet the argument, taken literally, predicts a good deal more failure than anyone observes. Second-hand cars are bought and sold in enormous numbers, as are houses, insurance policies and the services of lawyers, though in each of these one side knows more than the other. The interesting question is therefore not why markets with unevenly shared information can collapse, but why most of them do not. The answer is that commerce has developed devices that make private knowledge public, or at least costly to fake. A warranty is worth offering only to someone confident of the product; a brand is a hostage to future sales; a degree is useful to an employer because it is cheap to earn for those who are able and expensive for those who are not.

These devices are best regarded as substitutes for trust rather than as proofs of quality, and they carry costs of their own. A signal that anyone can send conveys nothing, so a signal must be expensive enough to deter the impostor, which means that the genuine article is obliged to pay for it too. Resources spent on proving worth, whether in credentials pursued for their value to employers rather than for what they teach, or in inspections that merely duplicate one another, are not available for anything else. Worse, the signals themselves invite imitation: where ratings carry weight, an industry in fake ratings appears, and the information that was supposed to reduce suspicion becomes one more thing to be suspicious of.

None of this diminishes the force of Akerlof's insight; it relocates it. The insight is less a prediction of vanished markets than a demonstration that markets function only when someone has paid to make information believable, and that the payment, borne in the end by buyers and sellers alike, is rarely recorded as a cost of doing business. A market that appears to run smoothly may therefore be running well only because a great deal of effort is being devoted, out of sight, to the problem it is said not to have.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.t: Markets in which sellers know more than buyers survive through costly devices that make information believable, and those costs usually go unrecorded.
options.why: This covers the unravelling (paragraph 1), the question of why most markets survive (paragraph 2), the costs of the remedies (paragraph 3) and the relocated insight (paragraph 4).

options.t: Akerlof's claim that markets with unevenly shared information collapse is refuted by the many such markets that continue to function.
options.why: Paragraph 4 says his insight is relocated, not diminished; the survival of markets is explained rather than used against him.

options.t: The disappearance of good used cars shows that warranties, brands and ratings should be abandoned in favour of direct inspection by buyers.
options.why: The author describes these devices as costly but never proposes abandoning them, and inspection is itself said to be wasteful when duplicated.

options.t: Unevenly shared information matters chiefly in markets for used goods, where sellers have both the incentive and the means to conceal defects.
options.why: Paragraph 2 lists houses, insurance and legal services; used cars are only the opening illustration.

questions.stem: The author refers to 'an industry in fake ratings' in order to:

options.t: warn that online commerce is less trustworthy than traditional trade because anonymity eases deception.
options.why: The passage does not compare online and traditional trade.

options.t: suggest that ratings should give way to certificates, which are rather more difficult to counterfeit.
options.why: No such recommendation is made; certificates are not offered as a replacement for ratings.

options.t: show that devices created to overcome suspicion can themselves become new objects of suspicion.
options.why: The sentence ends by saying the information meant to reduce suspicion becomes one more thing to be suspicious of.

options.t: argue that ratings, unlike warranties and brands, cannot work as signals because they cost nothing to send.
options.why: The author does not single ratings out as useless; the point is that any signal that carries weight invites imitation and so becomes a new source of suspicion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT offered in the passage as a device that helps make private information believable?

options.t: a warranty offered by a seller confident of the product.
options.why: Paragraph 2 names the warranty.

options.t: a discount offered to buyers who agree to pay in advance.
options.why: Discounts for advance payment are never mentioned; the passage lists warranties, brands, degrees, inspections and ratings.

options.t: a brand whose value the firm would forfeit by disappointing buyers.
options.why: Paragraph 2 calls a brand a hostage to future sales.

options.t: a degree that costs the able little and others a great deal.
options.why: Paragraph 2 names the degree on exactly this ground.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is the closest parallel to the process described in the first paragraph?

options.t: Bakers in a small town raise their prices after a poor harvest, and customers respond by buying noticeably less bread.
options.why: Here prices respond to costs and nothing is hidden from buyers.

options.t: A tailor attracts custom by displaying a framed certificate from a respected guild, and rivals begin to display their own.
options.why: This parallels the devices of paragraph 2, which are a remedy for the problem, not the unravelling itself.

options.t: An art dealer sells a forgery to a collector who cannot distinguish it from a genuine work, and is later prosecuted.
options.why: This is fraud in a single sale; no cycle of withdrawal and falling quality follows.

options.t: A health scheme charges one premium to everyone; the healthy leave as it rises, the pool worsens, and it rises again.
options.why: Better risks withdraw because the common price undervalues them, the quality of those who remain falls, and the price rises: the same spiral as in the used-car market.

recall.q: According to the passage, why do owners of better-than-average cars withdraw from the market?
options: The price offered reflects average quality and so undervalues their cars.
Dealers refuse to buy cars whose history cannot be inspected.
Warranties make it cheaper for them to keep their cars than to sell.
Insurers charge more to cover cars that are sold privately.

recall.q: Why, in the author's account, must a signal be expensive to send?
options: Expensive signals are the only ones that buyers have time to read.
Cheap signals are usually produced by firms unsure of their own products.
A signal anyone can send cannot separate the genuine seller from the impostor.
Governments require sellers to pay for any information given to buyers.

title: A natural experiment on the minimum wage
paras: For most of the twentieth century the economics of the minimum wage was an application of a result so elementary that it was taught before most students had met a regression. A legal floor above the wage that employers would otherwise pay prices some workers out of jobs; the only open question was how many. The conclusion owed its authority less to evidence than to the coherence of the theory from which it came, and results that sat awkwardly with it were more often blamed on flaws in the data than on flaws in the theory. A prediction that cannot be embarrassed by observation has ceased to be a prediction and become a presumption, and presumptions are what natural experiments exist to test.

The test arrived in 1992, when New Jersey raised its minimum wage and neighbouring Pennsylvania left its own alone. David Card and Alan Krueger telephoned fast-food outlets in both states before and after the increase, reasoning that restaurants on either side of a border share the same customers, the same weather and the same economic fortunes, so that Pennsylvania's experience would indicate what New Jersey's would have been without the law. The comparison could scarcely have been cleaner, and the result was unwelcome to many: employment in New Jersey had not fallen relative to that in Pennsylvania and, if anything, had grown a little. Critics promptly challenged the survey, producing payroll records that suggested a small decline, and the argument over whose figures were more reliable has never been wholly settled.

What survives the dispute is less a number than a way of arguing. The study did not show that minimum wages are harmless; it showed that the question is an empirical one whose answer depends on the market in which it is asked. If employers compete for labour, a floor above the going wage will cost jobs, as the textbook says. If, on the other hand, a few firms dominate local hiring, so that workers who ask for more can be replaced only at some inconvenience and have few places to go, the firm pays less than a worker's labour is worth, and a modest increase can raise pay without any loss of employment, because it takes from profit what it gives to wages. Which description fits a given town is a matter of fact, and the evidence suggests that both occur.

It would be as rash to treat the New Jersey result as a vindication as to treat it as an aberration. Studies of moderate increases have, in the main, found little effect on jobs, which is what the second description predicts, but they are silent about increases far outside the range of experience, where the first description presumably reasserts itself. Defenders of minimum wages are tempted to overlook this silence, and their opponents to exaggerate it. The sensible inference is neither that the floor is costless nor that it is costly, but that economists who confidently claimed to know in advance were claiming more than the theory entitled them to.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.t: The New Jersey study overturned the textbook view by showing that moderate increases in the minimum wage leave employment unchanged.
options.why: The author says the textbook result still holds where employers compete for labour, and that treating the study as a vindication would be rash; it made the question empirical rather than overturning the theory.

options.t: A natural experiment showed that the employment effect of a minimum wage depends on the market concerned, undermining confident prediction from theory alone.
options.why: This combines the study (paragraph 2), the argument that the answer depends on the kind of market (paragraph 3) and the caution against confident claims (paragraph 4).

options.t: Because the New Jersey figures remain disputed, the study's lasting value lies in its method, which later studies used to confirm the textbook prediction.
options.why: The author does say its method outlived the dispute, but later studies of moderate increases mostly found little effect on jobs, which fits the second description, not the textbook one.

options.t: The results are best explained by a few firms dominating local hiring, which suggests that the textbook's competitive model rarely fits real labour markets.
options.why: The author says the evidence suggests both kinds of market occur and does not judge how often the competitive one fits; the main point concerns confident prediction from theory.

questions.stem: The author would regard the claim that 'a minimum wage of any size can be imposed without loss of jobs' as:

options.t: justified by the New Jersey study, since its comparison of neighbouring states was about as clean as such comparisons can be.
options.why: A clean comparison shows what followed one moderate increase, not what a much larger one would do; the author says the evidence is silent about increases far outside experience.

options.t: a plausible extension of the explanation based on local hiring power, in which a floor takes from profit what it gives to wages.
options.why: Even where a few firms dominate hiring, the author says only a modest increase can raise pay without job losses; a floor of any size goes beyond both that explanation and the evidence.

options.t: at odds with the author's view only if payroll records are preferred to survey data.
options.why: The caution in paragraph 4 rests on the range of the evidence, not on which data set is preferred.

options.t: unsupported, because the evidence concerns moderate increases and says little about much larger ones.
options.why: Paragraph 4: studies of moderate increases are silent about increases far outside the range of experience.

questions.stem: The author's remark that a prediction 'that cannot be embarrassed by observation has ceased to be a prediction and become a presumption' is intended to:

options.t: criticise treating the competitive model's conclusion as settled whatever the data showed.
options.why: The sentence describes how the textbook conclusion was shielded from contrary evidence (paragraph 1).

options.t: argue that a theory should be discarded as soon as a single study contradicts it.
options.why: The author warns against treating the New Jersey result as vindication (paragraph 4), so no such rule is endorsed.

options.t: suggest that early studies contradicting the textbook were dismissed because their data were in fact poorer.
options.why: The author's complaint is that awkward results were blamed on the data by reflex, to protect the theory; the remark does not say that the data were actually worse.

options.t: argue that economic theories should not be taught until natural experiments have confirmed their predictions.
options.why: The remark concerns one conclusion treated as settled whatever the evidence showed; it sets no condition for teaching theory in general.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why employment did not fall in New Jersey?

options.t: Fast-food restaurants in New Jersey tended to employ somewhat younger workers than comparable restaurants in Pennsylvania did.
options.why: A difference in worker age bears on comparability, not on whether employers had power over wages.

options.t: Surveys conducted by telephone are generally less reliable than studies that rely on payroll records held by employers.
options.why: This concerns the quality of the data, the subject of the dispute in paragraph 2, not the explanation offered in paragraph 3.

options.t: Border-region workers could easily move between competing restaurants, so any employer paying less quickly lost staff.
options.why: If employers could not pay less without losing workers, they lacked the power over wages on which the explanation depends.

options.t: Later studies of much larger increases in the minimum wage found substantial job losses in several low-wage industries.
options.why: The author already says the evidence is limited to moderate increases; this is consistent with the explanation.

recall.q: Why did Card and Krueger survey outlets on both sides of the state border?
options: Pennsylvania had raised its minimum wage a year before New Jersey did so.
Restaurants in New Jersey refused to take part unless Pennsylvania's were included.
They wanted to compare pay in fast food with pay in other industries.
Pennsylvania's neighbouring outlets showed what New Jersey's would have experienced without the increase.

recall.q: What, according to the author, do studies of moderate increases leave unanswered?
options: Whether employers have any power over the wages they pay.
Whether the New Jersey survey was conducted fairly and consistently.
What happens when increases are far outside the range of experience.
Whether competitive labour markets exist anywhere in low-wage industries.

title: Beyond the tragedy of the commons
paras: Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay on the commons has been read so often as a parable about herdsmen that its actual structure is easily forgotten. Hardin asked what happens when a resource is open to all and each user captures the whole of the gain from taking more while bearing only a fraction of the cost. His answer, that users will take until the resource is ruined, followed from the assumptions with the rigour of a theorem, and it would be wrong to think that Elinor Ostrom, whose work is usually offered as its refutation, ever disputed the logic. What she disputed was the generalisation that the theorem was made to bear: that shared resources must therefore be either privatised or placed under the control of the state. The leap from 'can' to 'must', she suspected, was where the argument went astray.

The evidence she assembled was unglamorous. Alpine pastures in Switzerland and forests in Japan had been held in common for centuries, in some instances outlasting the political regimes around them; irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines distributed scarce water among farmers who answered to no single owner. If Hardin were right, these should have collapsed long ago. They had not, and the reason was not that their users were unusually virtuous but that they had devised rules. Hardin's herdsmen inhabit a pasture without boundaries, without monitors and without any means of punishing a trespasser, which is to say a pasture that is not a commons at all but an open-access resource, a distinction that his essay blurred and that she insisted upon.

From a comparison of many such cases, successful and unsuccessful, she drew a short list of regularities. Successful arrangements specified who could use the resource and who could not; gave those bound by the rules a hand in framing them; ensured that users watched one another; imposed sanctions that began lightly and grew with repetition; and provided inexpensive means of settling quarrels. The graduated sanction is the most instructive of these, because it reflects an understanding of how cooperation fails. A first breach is often an error, and punishing it harshly would convert a lapse into a grievance and the grievance into a dispute, whereas a light penalty announces that the rule is in force without rupturing the relationship that sustains it.

It would be wrong, however, to read Ostrom's findings as showing that communities can generally be trusted with their commons. The cases she studied were, almost by definition, ones in which cooperation had endured long enough to be studied, and the failures she included are a reminder that survivorship flatters. Her regularities describe small groups whose members know one another, can watch one another and expect to deal with one another again; they offer little purchase on the atmosphere or the oceans, where these conditions do not hold. Her achievement was more modest, and more lasting. She replaced a choice between two remedies with a question about institutions: under what rules, framed by whom, and enforced how, does a resource survive its users?

questions.stem: Which one of the following best summarises the author's view of Ostrom's contribution?

options.t: She showed that Hardin's analysis of open-access resources was mistaken and that communities may therefore be trusted to manage resources without outside rules.
options.why: Paragraph 1 says she did not dispute the logic, and paragraph 4 cautions against concluding that communities can generally be trusted.

options.t: She showed that community management outperforms privatisation and state control wherever users can watch one another and settle disputes cheaply.
options.why: The passage lists conditions shared by successful commons, but it never compares community management with private or state ownership in those settings.

options.t: She accepted Hardin's logic but showed that his conclusion depends on the absence of rules, shifting attention to institutions that make sharing last.
options.why: Paragraph 1 says she did not dispute the logic; paragraph 2 locates the gap in the absence of rules; paragraph 4 describes her achievement as a question about institutions.

options.t: She established principles from small communities that can be applied without modification to global problems such as the depletion of the oceans.
options.why: Paragraph 4 says her regularities offer little purchase on the atmosphere or the oceans.

questions.stem: The author's distinction between a 'commons' and an 'open-access resource' implies that:

options.t: Hardin's conclusion may hold for resources open to all without rules but not for those managed by a defined group.
options.why: A pasture with no boundaries, monitors or sanctions is open-access; Hardin's result concerns that case, not resources whose users have devised rules.

options.t: resources held in common, unlike open-access ones, are protected from overuse by the rules that their users devise.
options.why: The distinction says rules make survival possible, not that they guarantee it; the author notes that Ostrom's cases included failures and that survivorship flatters.

options.t: Hardin misjudged the incentives that lead individual herders to keep adding animals to a pasture that all may use.
options.why: The author says Ostrom did not dispute the logic of those incentives (paragraph 1).

options.t: Hardin's remedies of privatisation and state control suit open-access resources, while Ostrom's findings suit commons.
options.why: The distinction limits where Hardin's logic holds; it does not endorse privatisation or state control as the remedy for open-access resources, which the passage never assesses.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is a regularity Ostrom found in successful arrangements EXCEPT:

options.t: rules specifying which people may use the resource.
options.why: Paragraph 3: successful arrangements specified who could use the resource and who could not.

options.t: a role for those bound by the rules in framing them.
options.why: Paragraph 3: those bound by the rules had a hand in framing them.

options.t: penalties that begin lightly and grow with repetition.
options.why: Paragraph 3: sanctions began lightly and grew with repetition.

options.t: inspection and punishment by an authority outside the group.
options.why: Paragraph 3 says users watched one another; outside inspection and punishment is never listed.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's reservation about applying Ostrom's regularities to global problems?

options.t: Several of the communities Ostrom studied had adopted written rules before the resource showed any sign of depletion.
options.why: This concerns when rules were adopted, not whether they work at larger scale.

options.t: Within the communities studied, cooperation weakened sharply once membership grew large or members ceased to expect further dealings.
options.why: The regularities are said to depend on small, familiar groups with repeated dealings; evidence that cooperation weakens without those conditions supports the reservation.

options.t: Some of the commons Ostrom studied had been supervised for decades by officials of a distant central government.
options.why: This would complicate her findings about self-organisation, but says nothing about how they apply at global scale.

options.t: Hardin's essay remains among the most frequently cited in the social sciences, including in recent studies of fisheries.
options.why: Citation counts have no bearing on whether Ostrom's regularities scale up.

recall.q: What, according to the author, did Ostrom dispute in Hardin's argument?
options: The generalisation that shared resources must be privatised or state-controlled.
The assumption that each user captures the gain from taking more.
The claim that users bear only a fraction of the cost of overuse.
The logic by which unrestricted use leads to ruin of the resource.

recall.q: Why does the author call the graduated sanction 'the most instructive' principle?
options: It is the only principle that appears in every successful case that she examined.
First breaches are often errors, and harshness would erode the relationship that sustains cooperation.
It permits outside authorities to take over the management of a resource when it fails.
It makes monitoring by users unnecessary once the penalties have been announced.
